content: Pickled tofu, also known as tofu cheese, preserved tofu, or fermented tofu, is a type of processed and preserved tofu commonly used in Chinese cuisine. Production To produce pickled tofu, cubes of dried tofu are allowed to fully air-dry under hay, during which they slowly ferment due to exposure to airborne bacteria and fungal spores. Once the tofu has undergone this dry fermentation process, it is soaked in a brine solution. This brine is often enhanced with ingredients such as Chinese rice wine, vinegar, chili peppers, sesame oil, or a paste made from rice and soybeans. For red pickled tofu, red yeast rice, which is cultivated with the fungus Monascus purpureus, is added to impart its characteristic red color. Pickled tofu is typically sold in small glass jars. Characteristics Pickled tofu has a unique texture and mouthfeel that is reminiscent of certain dairy products. This is due to the breakdown of its proteins during the air-drying and fermentation process. On its own, pickled tofu does not have a strong odor, but it absorbs the flavors and aromas of the liquid in which it is soaked. Its texture and taste are often compared to a firm, smooth paste, similar to creamy blue cheese. In fact, it is sometimes referred to as Chinese cheese in English. When stored in a refrigerator, pickled tofu can be preserved for several years, during which its flavor is believed to improve over time. Use Pickled tofu is commonly used in small amounts, along with a bit of its soaking liquid, to flavor stir-fried or braised vegetable dishes, particularly leafy greens such as water spinach. It is also frequently consumed directly as a condiment, paired with rice or congee. Notes The Hwang Ryh Shang Company of Taiwan, a major producer of pickled tofu, has been noted to mislabel red yeast rice as red date (jujube) on the English ingredient list of its product labels, despite correctly listing 紅糟 (red yeast rice) in the Chinese ingredient list on the same product.
